who-whs-2023-p015-fig1.1:
Figure 1.1 Maternal mortality ratio and the average annual rate of reduction by WHO region, 2000–2020

This is a bar and scatter plot showing the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) and maternal mortality ratio (MMR) for different WHO regions.

The x-axis lists the WHO regions: European Region, Western Pacific Region, Region of the Americas, South-East Asia Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and African Region.

The left y-axis represents the Average annual rate of reduction (ARR), %, ranging from -4.0% to 8.0%.
The right y-axis represents the MMR (maternal deaths per 100 000 live births), ranging from 0 to 800.

The legend categories are:
- ARR, 2000–2015 (light blue bars)
- ARR 2016–2020 (orange bars)
- MMR, 2000 (green dots)
- MMR, 2020 (purple dots)

Data values:
European Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 4.9%
  - ARR 2016–2020: -2.4%
  - MMR, 2000: 20
  - MMR, 2020: 10
Western Pacific Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 4.0%
  - ARR 2016–2020: -2.8%
  - MMR, 2000: 60
  - MMR, 2020: 40
Region of the Americas:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 1.0%
  - ARR 2016–2020: -3.6%
  - MMR, 2000: 70
  - MMR, 2020: 60
South-East Asia Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 6.1%
  - ARR 2016–2020: 4.5%
  - MMR, 2000: 380
  - MMR, 2020: 130
Eastern Mediterranean Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 3.8%
  - ARR 2016–2020: 1.9%
  - MMR, 2000: 390
  - MMR, 2020: 190
African Region:
  - ARR, 2000–2015: 1.9%
  - ARR 2016–2020: 1.8%
  - MMR, 2000: 790
  - MMR, 2020: 540

Main comparisons and trends:
- The South-East Asia Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 (6.1%) and also the highest positive ARR from 2016–2020 (4.5%).
- The European Region had the highest ARR from 2000–2015 among regions with negative ARR in 2016-2020.
- The Region of the Americas had the most negative ARR from 2016–2020 (-3.6%).
- The African Region had the highest MMR in both 2000 (790) and 2020 (540).
- The European Region had the lowest MMR in both 2000 (20) and 2020 (10).
- All regions showed a decrease in MMR from 2000 to 2020.
- European Region, Western Pacific Region, and Region of the Americas experienced a negative ARR from 2016–2020, indicating an increase in maternal mortality during this period.
who-whs-2023-p016-fig1.2:
This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.2 Maternal mortality ratio by country/area, 2020".

The map displays the maternal mortality ratio (per 100 000 live births) for countries and areas worldwide in 2020.

The legend categories for the maternal mortality ratio are:
- ≥1000 (dark red)
- 500–999 (red)
- 300–499 (dark pink)
- 100–299 (medium pink)
- 20–99 (light pink)
- <20 (very light pink)
- No data available (light grey)
- Not applicable (grey)

A scale bar indicates distances in kilometers: 0, 1000, 2000, 4000 km.

The highest maternal mortality ratios (≥1000, dark red) are concentrated in Central Africa, including countries like Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia. Other countries in this category include Afghanistan and Yemen.

Countries with ratios between 500–999 (red) are also predominantly in Africa, such as Niger, Mali, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Sudan. Some countries in South Asia, like Pakistan, also fall into this category.

The lowest maternal mortality ratios (<20, very light pink) are observed across North America (Canada, United States), most of Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and parts of East Asia (e.g., Japan, South Korea). Many countries in South America also show lower ratios, generally in the 20–99 or 100–299 range.

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland, Western Sahara, and some parts of Central Asia. "Not applicable" (grey) is shown for areas like the Arctic.

Overall, the map clearly shows a strong geographical disparity, with the highest maternal mortality ratios concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, while North America, Europe, and Oceania generally have the lowest ratios.
who-whs-2023-p017-fig1.3:
This figure consists of two line charts, stacked vertically, showing trends in adolescent birth rates by age group and WHO region from 2000 to 2022.

Panel 1: Adolescent girls, 15–19 years
The y-axis represents "Birth rate (per 1000 adolescent girls 15–19 years)" ranging from 0 to 140. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2022.
The legend categories are: African Region (red), Region of the Americas (light blue), Eastern Mediterranean Region (green), European Region (orange), South-East Asia Region (purple), Western Pacific Region (yellow), and Global (grey).

Key trends:
- African Region shows the highest birth rates throughout the period, starting around 120 in 2000 and declining to just over 100 by 2022.
- Region of the Americas starts around 85 in 2000 and declines steadily to around 40 by 2022.
- South-East Asia Region shows a significant drop, starting around 60 in 2000, decreasing sharply around 2005, and continuing to decline to below 20 by 2022.
- Eastern Mediterranean Region and Global rates are in the middle, showing a general decline.
- European Region and Western Pacific Region consistently show the lowest birth rates, generally below 20, with the European Region slightly higher than the Western Pacific Region. All regions show a declining trend over the period.

Panel 2: Adolescent girls, 10–14 years
The y-axis represents "Birth rate (per 1000 adolescent girls 10–14 years)" ranging from 0 to 10. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2022.
The legend categories are the same as Panel 1.

Key trends:
- African Region shows the highest birth rates, starting around 8.5 in 2001 and declining to just over 5 by 2022.
- South-East Asia Region starts around 4.5 in 2000, drops sharply around 2005, and continues to decline to below 1 by 2022.
- Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and Global rates are in the middle, all showing a declining trend and converging towards lower values.
- European Region and Western Pacific Region consistently show the lowest birth rates, generally below 1, with the Western Pacific Region being the lowest. All regions show a declining trend over the period.
who-whs-2023-p019-fig1.4:
This is a line chart titled "Figure 1.4 Trends in the global under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" ranging from 0 to 80.
The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021, with labels at 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2021.
The chart background is divided into two shaded regions: a green-shaded region from 2000 to 2010, and a red-shaded region from 2010 to 2021.

There are two lines in the chart:
- A light blue line represents "U5MR" (under-five mortality rate).
- A purple line represents "NMR" (neonatal mortality rate).

Data values and trends:
For U5MR (light blue line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 4.0%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.7%.
The U5MR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 78 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 38 per 1000 live births in 2021.

For NMR (purple line):
- In the 2000-2010 period (green-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 3.2%.
- In the 2010-2021 period (red-shaded), the average annual rate of reduction (ARR) is 2.2%.
The NMR shows a continuous decrease from approximately 30 per 1000 live births in 2000 to approximately 18 per 1000 live births in 2021.

Overall trends:
Both U5MR and NMR show a decreasing trend from 2000 to 2021.
The rate of reduction for both U5MR and NMR was higher in the 2000-2010 period compared to the 2010-2021 period.
U5MR is consistently higher than NMR throughout the entire period.
who-whs-2023-p019-fig1.5:
This is a stacked area chart titled "Figure 1.5 Trends in neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths, by WHO region, 2000–2021".

The y-axis represents "Deaths (millions)" ranging from 0 to 10. The x-axis represents years from 2000 to 2021.

The chart is divided into two main stacked sections:
1.  "Neonatal deaths (0–28 days)" at the bottom.
2.  "Post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months)" on top of the neonatal deaths.

Each of these two sections is further subdivided by WHO region, represented by different colors in the legend:
*   African Region (red)
*   South-East Asia Region (purple)
*   Eastern Mediterranean Region (green)
*   Region of the Americas (light blue)
*   European Region (orange)
*   Western Pacific Region (yellow)

There are also two global trend lines:
*   Global under-five deaths (solid purple line)
*   Global neonatal deaths (dashed purple line)

The chart shows a clear downward trend in both neonatal deaths and post-neonatal under-five deaths from 2000 to 2021.

In 2000, the total global under-five deaths were approximately 10 million. By 2021, this figure had decreased to approximately 5 million.

For neonatal deaths (0–28 days):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 3.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.2 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region contribute the largest proportions to neonatal deaths throughout the period.

For post-neonatal under-five deaths (1–59 months):
*   In 2000, the total was approximately 6.5 million.
*   In 2021, the total was approximately 2.8 million.
The African Region and South-East Asia Region also contribute the largest proportions to post-neonatal under-five deaths.

The overall trend for both categories and all regions is a decrease in deaths over the 21-year period. The African Region consistently shows the largest number of deaths in both categories.
who-whs-2023-p020-fig1.6:
This is a choropleth map titled "Figure 1.6 Under-five mortality rate and neonatal mortality rate, by country/area, 2021". The map displays two types of mortality rates for countries and areas worldwide in 2021.

The "Under-five mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by color-coded regions:
- >75: Dark purple
- 51-75: Purple
- 26-50: Pink
- ≤25: Light orange
- No data available: Light grey
- Not applicable: Dark grey

The "Neonatal mortality rate (per 1000 live births)" is represented by circles of varying sizes and colors:
- 40: Largest red circle
- 29: Medium red circle
- 18: Small red circle
- 12: Medium green circle
- 1: Smallest green circle

The map shows that countries in sub-Saharan Africa generally have the highest under-five mortality rates (>75 and 51-75, dark purple and purple regions) and also the highest neonatal mortality rates (largest red circles, 40 and 29). Examples include Chad, Central African Republic, Somalia, and Nigeria.

Conversely, most countries in North America, Europe, Australia, and parts of Asia have the lowest under-five mortality rates (≤25, light orange regions) and the lowest neonatal mortality rates (smallest green circles, 1 and 12). Some countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia, such as India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, show a mix of pink (26-50) and light orange (≤25) for under-five mortality, with varying neonatal mortality rates, including some red circles (18 and 29).

Countries with "No data available" (light grey) include Greenland and parts of the Sahara desert. "Not applicable" (dark grey) is shown for some small island nations and territories.
who-whs-2023-p023-fig1.7:
Figure 1.7 is a multi-panel line chart showing the probability of dying from four major NCDs* (ages 30–69 years) from 2000 to 2048, with projections versus the SDG target for different WHO regions and globally.

The figure consists of six panels, each representing a different WHO region or the global average: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.

The y-axis for all panels is "Probability of dying between ages 30 and 69 years (%)", ranging from 5 to 30. The x-axis for all panels is "Year", ranging from 2000 to 2050, with tick marks every 10 years.

The legend categories are:
- Observed (solid purple line)
- Projected based on observed trends 2000–2019 (dashed blue line)
- Required trajectory in 2019–2030 to meet the SDG3.4.1 Target (dashed green line)

Main trends visible:
- In all regions and globally, the "Observed" probability of dying from NCDs has been decreasing from 2000 to 2019.
- The "Projected based on observed trends 2000–2019" line shows a continued decrease in all regions, but at a slower rate than the "Required trajectory in 2019–2030 to meet the SDG3.4.1 Target".
- In all panels, the "Required trajectory" line shows a steeper decline than the "Projected based on observed trends" line, indicating that current trends are not sufficient to meet the SDG target.
- The European Region generally shows the highest observed probability of dying from NCDs, starting above 25% in 2000 and decreasing to around 18% by 2019.
- The African Region and South-East Asia Region also show high observed probabilities, starting around 25% in 2000.
- The Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and Western Pacific Region show intermediate observed probabilities, starting around 18-20% in 2000.
- The "Global" panel reflects an average trend, starting around 22% in 2000 and decreasing to around 17% by 2019.

* Cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease and diabetes.
Source: Ref. (2).

who-whs-2023-p026-fig1.10:
This figure is a multi-panel line chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of obesity among adults (age 18 years or older) across different WHO regions and globally, from 1975 to 2016.

The figure consists of seven panels, each representing a different region or the global average: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.

The y-axis for all panels represents "Prevalence (%)" ranging from 0 to 35 in increments of 5. The x-axis for all panels represents years, with labels for 1975, 1985, 1995, 2005, and 2016.

There are three lines in each panel, distinguished by color, representing different categories:
- Light blue line: Both sexes
- Orange line: Male
- Purple line: Female

Main trends and comparisons:
Across all regions and globally, the prevalence of obesity has consistently increased from 1975 to 2016 for both sexes, males, and females.

In most regions, the prevalence of obesity is higher among females than males, with the purple line (Female) generally above the orange line (Male). The light blue line (Both sexes) falls between the male and female lines.

Region-specific observations (approximate values based on visual estimation, as no specific data labels are provided):
- **African Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.
- **Region of the Americas:** Shows the highest prevalence among all regions. In 2016, female obesity prevalence is over 30%, male around 25%, and both sexes around 28%.
- **Eastern Mediterranean Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 15%, and both sexes around 20%.
- **European Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 25%, male around 20%, and both sexes around 22%.
- **South-East Asia Region:** Shows the lowest prevalence among all regions. In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 5%, male around 3%, and both sexes around 4%.
- **Western Pacific Region:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 7%, male around 5%, and both sexes around 6%.
- **Global:** In 2016, female obesity prevalence is around 15%, male around 10%, and both sexes around 12%.

The Region of the Americas consistently shows the highest prevalence of obesity throughout the period, while the South-East Asia Region consistently shows the lowest prevalence. The rate of increase appears steepest in the Region of the Americas and Eastern Mediterranean Region.
who-whs-2023-p027-fig1.11:
Figure 1.11 is a multi-panel line chart showing the age-standardized prevalence of hypertension among adults (age 30–79 years) across different WHO regions and globally, from 1990 to 2019.

The figure consists of seven panels, each representing a different region or the global average: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, Western Pacific Region, and Global.

The y-axis for all panels represents "Prevalence (%)" ranging from 0 to 50 in increments of 5. The x-axis for all panels represents years: 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2019.

The legend indicates three line categories:
- Light blue line: Both sexes
- Orange line: Male
- Purple line: Female

**Observed Trends and Comparisons:**

**African Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Female prevalence (purple line) is consistently higher than male prevalence (orange line).
- In 2010, female prevalence peaked at approximately 31%, male at approximately 27%, and both sexes at approximately 29%.

**Region of the Americas:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Female prevalence (purple line) is consistently lower than male prevalence (orange line).
- In 2010, male prevalence peaked at approximately 29.5%, female at approximately 24%, and both sexes at approximately 27%.

**Eastern Mediterranean Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then slightly decreased by 2019.
- Female prevalence (purple line) is consistently higher than male prevalence (orange line).
- In 2010, female prevalence peaked at approximately 31%, male at approximately 28%, and both sexes at approximately 29.5%.

**European Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females consistently decreased from 1990 to 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 1990, male prevalence was highest at approximately 42%, female at approximately 38%, and both sexes at approximately 40%.
- In 2019, male prevalence was lowest at approximately 34%, female at approximately 22%, and both sexes at approximately 28%. This region shows the most significant decline.

**South-East Asia Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females consistently increased from 1990 to 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 2019, male prevalence was highest at approximately 22%, female at approximately 20%, and both sexes at approximately 21%.

**Western Pacific Region:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 2010, male prevalence peaked at approximately 30%, female at approximately 24%, and both sexes at approximately 27%.

**Global:**
- Prevalence for both sexes, males, and females increased from 1990 to 2010, then decreased by 2019.
- Male prevalence (orange line) is consistently higher than female prevalence (purple line).
- In 2010, male prevalence peaked at approximately 26%, female at approximately 23%, and both sexes at approximately 24.5%.
- In 2019, male prevalence was approximately 23%, female at approximately 20.5%, and both sexes at approximately 22%.

Overall, the European Region shows a clear downward trend in hypertension prevalence across all categories, while the South-East Asia Region shows a consistent upward trend. Other regions and the global average show an initial increase followed by a decrease. Male prevalence is generally higher than female prevalence in most regions and globally, except for the African and Eastern Mediterranean Regions where female prevalence is higher.
who-whs-2023-p029-fig1.12:
Figure 1.12 is a composite figure showing reported COVID-19 deaths by WHO region.

The left panel is a horizontal bar chart showing total reported COVID-19 deaths by WHO region up to 11 March 2023.
The categories and their values are:
Region of the Americas: 2 936 906
European Region: 2 201 892
South-East Asia Region: 803 904
Western Pacific Region: 407 355
Eastern Mediterranean Region: 349 680
African Region: 175 315

The right panel is a stacked area chart showing the number of reported deaths over time, from January 2020 to March 2023.
The y-axis is "Number of reported deaths" ranging from 0 to 25 000.
The x-axis shows dates at approximately two-month intervals, starting from 1 January 2020 and ending at 1 March 2023.
The stacked areas are colored to correspond to the regions in the bar chart:
Region of the Americas: light blue
European Region: orange
South-East Asia Region: purple
Western Pacific Region: yellow
Eastern Mediterranean Region: green
African Region: red

Main trends visible in the stacked area chart:
The overall number of reported deaths shows several peaks. The highest peak appears to be around January-February 2021, with another significant peak around January-February 2022.

The South-East Asia Region (purple) shows a notable peak in mid-2021.

who-whs-2023-p030-fig1.13:
Figure 1.13 is a stacked bar chart showing total excess deaths by WHO region from 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2021.

The y-axis represents "Deaths (in millions)" ranging from 0 to 10.
The x-axis represents different WHO regions: African Region, Region of the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean Region, European Region, South-East Asia Region, and Western Pacific Region.

The legend indicates two categories:
- Light blue: "Reported COVID-19"
- Orange: "Excess deaths not captured in reported COVID-19 deaths"

Each bar represents the total excess deaths for a region, with the total value and uncertainty interval (UI) labelled above the bar. Error bars indicate the uncertainty interval.

Data values are as follows:
- African Region: Total: 0.8 (UI 0.5–1.1) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.2 million.
- Region of the Americas: Total: 3.2 (UI 3.2–3.3) million. Reported COVID-19: 2.4 million.
- Eastern Mediterranean Region: Total: 1.3 (UI 1.1–1.5) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.3 million.
- European Region: Total: 3.2 (UI 3.1–3.2) million. Reported COVID-19: 1.7 million.
- South-East Asia Region: Total: 6.1 (UI 4.7–7.8) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.7 million.
- Western Pacific Region: Total: 0.2 (UI 0–0.4) million. Reported COVID-19: 0.2 million.

Main comparisons:
- The South-East Asia Region has the highest total excess deaths at 6.1 million, with a large proportion of these being excess deaths not captured in reported COVID-19 deaths.
- The Western Pacific Region has the lowest total excess deaths at 0.2 million, with all of these being reported COVID-19 deaths.
- The Region of the Americas and European Region have the second highest total excess deaths, both at 3.2 million.
- For the African Region, Eastern Mediterranean Region, and South-East Asia Region, the orange segment (excess deaths not captured) is significantly larger than the light blue segment (reported COVID-19).
- For the Region of the Americas and European Region, both segments are substantial, with reported COVID-19 deaths being higher in the Americas (2.4 million) than in Europe (1.7 million).

who-whs-2023-p040-fig1.18:
Figure 1.18 Percentage of hot days (“heat stress”), Saint Lucia, 1900–2100*

This is a line chart showing the percentage of hot days over time in Saint Lucia.
The x-axis represents the Year, ranging from 1900 to 2100.
The y-axis represents the Percentage of hot days (%), ranging from 0 to 120.

The chart displays multiple lines:
- A blue line represents the annual and smoothed observed record. This line shows fluctuations, generally staying below 20% until around 1980, then rising to approximately 20% by 2000.
- Orange lines represent a high-emission scenario (Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5, RCP8.5). These lines show a sharp increase in the percentage of hot days, starting around 2000 and continuing to rise steeply towards 2100. By 2100, the orange lines indicate percentages ranging from approximately 80% to over 100%.
- Green lines represent a low-emission scenario (RCP2.6). These lines also show an increase, but at a slower rate than the high-emission scenario. By 2100, the green lines indicate percentages ranging from approximately 60% to 80%.
- Multiple grey lines represent individual global climate models, showing the spread of projections.

Main trends:
- The observed record (blue line) shows a slight increase in hot days from 1900 to 2000.
- Both emission scenarios project a significant increase in hot days from 2000 to 2100.
- The high-emission scenario (orange lines) projects a much steeper and higher increase in hot days compared to the low-emission scenario (green lines).
- By 2100, under the high-emission scenario, the percentage of hot days is projected to be significantly higher, with some models exceeding 100%, compared to the low-emission scenario.

Note: * The figure presents climate model projections for the percentage of “hot days”. A “hot day” is a day when the maximum temperature exceeds the 90th percentile threshold for the time of the year. The blue lines represent annual and smoothed observed record. The orange lines represent a high-emission scenario (Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5, RCP8.5) and the green lines represent a low-emission scenario (RCP2.6). The scenarios are presented across some 20 global climate models. The figure shows each model individually, as well as their average and the 90% model range (shaded).
